result:
There is a particular silence that only exists in the small hours before dawn. It isn't the absence of sound—it's the *holding* of sound, the way a still lake holds the image of a mountain. In that hour, the world seems to be waiting for something. A promise. A starting gun. The first bird that hasn't yet remembered to sing.

I've been thinking about firsts lately. Not the big ones, the kind carved into yearbooks and wedding albums, but the quiet ones. The first time a child sees snow and has no word for it yet, so they simply stare. The first time you taste a fruit you've eaten a hundred times but suddenly understand it—really understand it, as if the flavor had been hiding behind a curtain your whole life, waiting for the right morning to step out.

It's strange to think that everything we are is just a mosaic of these firsts, cemented together by repetition. The first step becomes a thousand steps. The first word becomes a language. The first heartbreak becomes a scar, then a story, then a lesson, then just a footnote in a biography you no longer recognize as your own.

We tend to mourn the loss of novelty. The world gets smaller as we get older; the magic of the unknown retreats like a tide. But I wonder if that's a misunderstanding. Perhaps novelty isn't lost—it's *translated*. What was once the thrill of discovery becomes the quieter thrill of depth. The first time you see the ocean is awe. The hundredth time you see it is something else entirely: it's the recognition that the ocean was never the same twice, and neither were you. The wave that crashes now is the only wave that has ever crashed exactly like this, and you are the only you who has ever stood exactly here.

That's the trick of it, isn't it? Every moment is a first. We just forget to look closely enough to notice. The first sip of coffee this morning was objectively a first—the beans, the water, the temperature, the precise state of your tongue and your mood and the slant of light through the window. It will never happen again. We just don't have the attention span to treat it as such.

There's an old parable about a monk who was asked what he did before enlightenment. "I chopped wood and carried water," he said. Asked what he did after, he replied: "I chopped wood and carried water." The difference, he explained, was that before, he was always somewhere else. After, he was in the wood. In the water. In the carrying.

I think that's what I want to practice. Not the grand search for meaning, but the willingness to show up for the ordinary, the repeated, the mundane—and to see them for what they truly are: unrepeatable gifts that will never occur again.

So perhaps today, when the silence holds its breath before the first bird sings, I'll pay attention. I'll notice the exact quality of the dark, the temperature of the air, the way the world leans slightly toward the sun like a flower turning its face.

Because this moment—right now, this very one—is a first. And it will only happen once.
